title: Log-concavity and tunneling: adiabatic quantum optimization for convex functions (with a spike)
authors: Arthur Braida, Elie Bermot, Simon Apers
abstract: Quantum tunneling is expected to provide a computational speedup in quantum computing, a phenomenon that Adiabatic Quantum Optimization (AQO) aims to leverage. While some academic proofs of concept have been studied, such as the "Hamming weight with a spike" (HWS) problem, the algorithmic gains of this effect remain underexplored. In this work we extend the analysis underlying HWS to more general potentials.   In the first half of the work, we establish (discrete) log-concavity of the ground state as a key structural property in this context. We devise a framework for establishing log-concavity of the ground state for a large family of discrete, 1-dimensional Schrödinger operators. The family includes convex potentials, but also certain potentials with local minima. In the convex case, this provides a discrete version of a continuous result by Brascamp and Lieb ('76). We demonstrate the utility of our result by establishing new spectral gap bounds, going beyond related results by Jarret and Jordan ('14) for convex potentials.   In the second half of the work, we use our results on log-concavity to extend the perturbative analysis of HWS by Reichardt ('04) to the larger family of potentials with log-concave ground state. As a concrete instantiation, we use our result to extend the HWS analysis from a linear potential (which is exactly solvable) to a quadratic potential (which is no longer solvable). Our result strongly suggests the broader applicability of tunneling to convex potentials with spikes
summary: The paper develops a framework using log-concavity properties to analyze quantum tunneling effects in Adiabatic Quantum Optimization. It extends these techniques from simple potentials to general convex functions, culminating in an efficient time complexity bound for solving the quadratic Hamming weight problem via quantum annealing.
main_problem: The work analyzes how quantum tunneling provides a computational speedup for Adiabatic Quantum Optimization (AQO) when minimizing complex cost functions, extending analysis beyond simple cases like the Hamming weight.
main_result: By establishing log-concavity of the ground state wavefunction, the authors derive new spectral gap bounds and show that the quadratic HWS problem can be solved in $O(n^4)$ time via AQO under specific spike conditions.
method: The methodology combines structural analysis (proving discrete log-concavity for Schrödinger operators) with perturbation theory applied to the spectral gap, linking these properties directly to computational complexity bounds.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by a 1D quantum Hamiltonian $H(s)$ interpolating between an initial state and a target potential $V$, often involving quadratic potentials ($V_q$) and localized spike perturbations ($h$).
key_observables: Spectral Gap ($\Delta$), Log-concavity/Ultra-log-concavity of the ground state wavefunction, Overlap $\left| \langle\psi_0|\varphi_mangleight|^2$.
important_parameters: The spike height ($ ar{h}$), the support boundaries ($\ell, u$), and the system size ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis heavily relies on establishing log-concavity of the ground state as a key structural property, which allows for bounding the spectral gap even in the presence of spikes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate potential energy landscapes (e.g., quadratic potentials) and show the overlap between the true ground state wavefunction and an optimal binomial ansatz state $|\varphi_mangle$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing log-concavity for a general family of Hamiltonians, then using this structural property to extend perturbative spike analysis (Reichardt's work) to quadratic potentials, culminating in the time complexity bound for the quadratic HWS problem.
why_interesting: This research provides rigorous mathematical tools (log-concavity bounds) to analyze quantum speedups in optimization problems, directly impacting the theoretical understanding of adiabatic quantum computation efficiency.
